A B S T R A C T
This study systematically investigates the tension–tension fatigue behavior and deformation mechanisms of
solution-treated and aging-treated Fe-30.5Mn-8Al-1C (wt%) austenitic low-density steels. focusing on the critical
role of κ-carbide precipitation state in controlling fatigue properties. In aged samples, intragranular κ-carbides
induce planar dislocation slip through a “glide plane softening” mechanism, enhancing slip reversibility under
cyclic loading and thereby improving fatigue life. Strengthening is primarily due to the interaction between
dislocations and intragranular k-carbides. An appropriate increase in the size of intragranular κ-carbides
significantly enhances fatigue life and fatigue strength at low stress amplitudes. Conversely, intergranular
κ-carbide precipitation impedes slip transmission, intensifies localized stress concentration, and accelerates
damage, thus reducing fatigue life at high stress amplitudes. These findings strongly demonstrate that acceler
ating the precipitation of intragranular κ-carbides while suppressing intergranular precipitation is an effective
microstructural pathway to concurrently enhance fatigue performance of Fe-Mn-Al-C austenitic low-density
steels across the entire range of stress amplitudes

ciency demands, the pursuit of automotive lightweighting has intensi
fied the search for materials with superior strength-to-weight ratios.
Low-density steels, especially Fe-Mn-Al-C alloys, have emerged as
promising candidates [1–5]. The addition of ~10 wt% aluminum re
duces density by approximately 10–13 % compared with conventional
steels, while maintaining or even enhancing strength–ductility synergy
[3,6–8]. Some previous studies have shown that optimized aging
treatment facilitates the uniform precipitation of high-density nanoscale
(Fe,Mn) AlC κ-carbides within the γ matrix through spinodal decom
position [9,10]. These intragranular κ-carbides provide pronounced
precipitation hardening [11–15]. However, high-temperature exposure
also triggers discontinuous precipitation and cellular transformation at
grain boundaries (GBs), leading to the formation of coarse intergranular
κ-carbides [16,17]. Such precipitates would concentrate interfacial
stress, degrade mechanical properties, and significantly compromise
alloy reliability [2,18]. Accordingly, tailoring κ-carbide precipitation to
achieve intragranular refinement while suppressing intergranular pre
cipitate coarsening is of critical importance for the performance
optimization.

structures and components [19,20]. As vehicle weight is reduced,

The present study systematically investigates the fatigue behavior of
an Fe-30.5Mn-8Al-1C (wt%) alloy under tension–tension cyclic loading.
By tailoring the morphology and distribution of κ-carbide precipitation
through controlled thermal treatments, the effects of both intragranular
and intergranular κ-carbides on the fatigue life, cyclic response, and
damage mechanisms are elucidated. This work is expected to provide
fundamental insights crucial for the development of fatigue-resistant,
high-strength, and low-density steels that are suitable for automotive
structural applications under severe cyclic loading conditions.
2. Experimental materials and methods
2.1. Materials
The investigated steel has a nominal composition of Fe-30.5Mn-8Al
1C (wt%). A 50 kg ingot was prepared by vacuum melting and subse
quently forged into a billet with a cross-section of 30 mm × 30 mm. The
billet was then hot-rolled to a final thickness of 4 mm. Solution treat
ment was conducted at 1050 <sup>◦</sup>C for 1 h, followed by water quenching to
room temperature; this condition is referred to as ST. To obtain different
precipitation states of intragranular and intergranular κ-carbides,
selected ST samples were further aged at 550 <sup>◦</sup>C, 600 <sup>◦</sup>C, and 650 <sup>◦</sup>C for
6 h, designated as 550-6, 600-6, and 650-6, respectively.
2.2. Mechanical tests
Flat dog-bone-shaped tensile samples were machined from the sheets
using wire electrical discharge machining (EDM), with their tensile axes
parallel to the rolling direction. A schematic of the shape and di
mensions of the tensile test samples is provided in Fig. 1. The sample
surfaces were mechanically polished and subsequently electro-polished

Flat dog-bone-shaped fatigue samples were also extracted from the
sheets via EDM, with the loading axis parallel to the rolling direction.
These samples shared the same dimensions as the tensile samples
(Fig. 1). The surfaces were prepared using the same procedure of me
chanical grinding and electropolishing to ensure a stress-free and
smooth finish. Stress-controlled tension–tension fatigue tests were con
ducted in ambient air using a servo-hydraulic fatigue testing machine
(Shimadzu EHF-EV050K2A-020-1). A sinusoidal waveform was adopted
in fatigue tests at a frequency of 20 Hz and a stress ratio of R = 0.1.
2.3. Microstructural characterizations
The microstructure of the undeformed ST sample was characterized
by electron backscatter diffraction (EBSD) on a TESCAN MIRA3 scan
ning electron microscope (SEM) equipped with an Oxford EBSD detec
tor. Prior to observations, the sample surface was prepared through
mechanical polishing followed by electropolishing. Transmission elec
tron microscopy (TEM) was conducted on a JEOL JEM-2100F micro
scope operating at 200 kV to characterize the precipitation of κ-carbides
in the aged samples (550-6, 600-6 and 650-6). TEM foils were prepared
by mechanically grinding slices to approximately 50 μm in thickness,
followed by twin-jet electropolishing in a solution of 8 vol.% perchloric
acid in ethanol at 30 V. The electrolyte was maintained at approximately
− 20 <sup>◦</sup>C to prevent sample oxidation.
For the post-fractured samples, the fracture surfaces and lateral
surfaces were examined using a JEOL JSM-7800F SEM. Furthermore,
EBSD was employed to analyze crack propagation path on externa
surfaces. These scans were acquired using a step size of 0.8 μm, and the
data were analyzed using AZtecCrystal post-processing software. To
gain further insight into the deformation mechanisms, the deformation
microstructures in the post-fractured samples were characterized by
TEM. TEM foils were extracted from the gauge sections of the deformed
specimens to ensure microstructural representativeness.
3. Results
3.1. Microstructures prior to deformation
Fig. 2 shows the microstructures in the ST and aged samples. The
inverse pole figure (IPF) map of the ST sample reveals a fully austenitic
microstructure (Fig. 2a). After aging, the 550-6 sample exhibits a high
density of nanoscale κ-carbides (~11 nm) with rectangular morphology,
uniformly precipitated within the austenite grains (Fig. 2b). With

<100> directions of the matrix (Fig. 2c). Concurrently, intergranular
κ-carbide precipitation is also observable. Further increasing aging
temperature to 650 <sup>◦</sup>C leads to coarsening of intragranular κ-carbides to
approximately 24 nm, accompanied by more pronounced intergranular
precipitation in the 650-6 sample (Fig. 2d). The size of intragranular
κ-carbides is quantified using an equivalent-circle diameter, and the
quantitative evolution of κ-carbide size with aging temperature is
summarized in Fig. 3. The detailed κ-carbide precipitation behavior of
the Fe-30.5Mn-8Al-1C alloy during aging treatment has been reported in
our previous work [6]. This microstructural overview provides the basis
for interpreting the subsequent fatigue behavior.

compared with the ST condition. Among the aged samples, 550-6 and

3.4. Fracture characteristics
Fig. 6 displays the macroscopic fatigue fracture surfaces of the Fe-
30.5Mn-8Al-1C steel tested at stress amplitudes of 180 and 315 MPa.
All samples exhibit a similar three-zone fracture morphology,
comprising the crack initiation, propagation, and rapid fracture regions,
with cracks initiating at the surface and propagating radially inward. At
a given stress amplitude, the area fraction (fa) of the crack initiation and
propagation zones (marked by yellow dashed lines in Fig. 6) is larger in
the aged samples than in the ST sample; it is consistent with their
extended fatigue life. The corresponding fa values were quantitatively
measured and are labeled in the upper-right corner of each subfigure.
Specifically, the 600-6 sample showed the largest area fraction at
180 MPa, while the 550-6 sample exhibited the highest at 315 MPa, in
line with their respective optimal fatigue resistance at low and high
stress amplitudes.
Fig. 7 illustrates high-magnification views of the fatigue crack
propagation zone in the ST, 550-6, 600-6, and 650-6 samples tested at
two stress amplitudes of 180 and 315 MPa. Well-defined fatigue stria
tions were observed in all samples, indicating transgranular crack
advancement via reversible dislocation slip on specific crystallographic
planes [27]. The formation of fatigue striations typically corresponds to
cyclic crack tip blunting during loading and re-sharpening during
unloading, and a reduced striation spacing indicates a lower crack
propagation rate [28–30]. Notably, the 550-6 and 600-6 samples exhibit
more pronounced and closely spaced striations, with the narrowest
spacing observed in the 550-6 sample at 315 MPa and in the 600-6
sample at 180 MPa. This corresponds to their respective longer fatigue
lives shown in Fig. 5.

4. Discussion
4.1. Impact of intragranular κ-carbides on dislocation slip mode
In the ST sample, the observed planar slip bands are primarily
attributed to the short-range ordering (SRO) structure within the
austenitic matrix. This observation aligns with the “glide plane soft
ening” effect proposed by Gerold and Karnthaler [40]. The strong C-Mn
chemical affinity leads to a non-random solute distribution, forming
locally ordered clusters [41–43]. When a leading dislocation cuts
through such an SRO region, it disrupts the local order and reduces the
resistance on that specific glide plane, thereby facilitating subsequent
coplanar glide and the formation of distinct planar slip bands [44–46].
However, because SRO structure is relatively weak and spatially het
erogeneous, repeated shearing by moving dislocations tends to destroy it
prematurely. The resulting non-uniform softening across potential slip
planes fosters local strain concentrations (Fig. 12a).
Aging treatment induces coherent ordered L1 -structured intra
granular κ-carbides that amplify “glide plane softening” effect beyond
the SRO level. When moving dislocations shear these precipitates [47],
anti-phase boundaries (APBs) are created. After a plane has been swept
and order locally disrupted, subsequent dislocations traverse the same
plane with reduced resistance because additional APBs are no longer
formed [42]. This path-dependent process channels dislocation activity
to a limited set of previously softened glide planes, strengthening slip
planarity and suppressing cross-slip. The uniform nanoscale dispersion
of κ-carbides promotes the homogeneous formation of planar slip bands
and distributes plastic strain over multiple coplanar systems, thereby
mitigating localized strain concentrations. Crucially, this enhanced slip
planarity and restricted cross-slip significantly improve the reversibility
of dislocation motion under cyclic loading [44]. Dislocations can more
readily retrace their path on well-defined softened planes during load
reversal, leading to reduced accumulated damage per cycle (Fig. 12b).
These mechanisms rationalize the superior fatigue performance of the
aged samples relative to the ST samples.

amplitudes

significant portion of the total fatigue life; strengthening the matrix is
therefore an effective route to delay initiation [48,49]. In Fe-Mn-Al-C
alloys, precipitation strengthening by intragranular κ-carbides is domi
nant, and the active dislocation-precipitate interaction depends on the
size of precipitates. The dominant mechanism transitions from shearing
to Orowan bypassing as the precipitate size increases, and a critical size
of approximately 27 nm was reported in analogous alloy systems [50].

resolution TEM (HRTEM) images of κ-carbides in the fatigued 550-6

4.3. Effect of intergranular κ-carbides on fatigue behavior at high stress
amplitudes
At high stress amplitudes, the activation of mobile dislocations be
comes more pronounced, and their interactions with grain boundaries
are more significant. Thus, the state of grain boundaries exerts a strong
influence on fatigue life [51]. Plastic deformation heterogeneity in
metallic materials predominantly arises from SFs mismatch between
adjacent grains. “Soft-oriented” grains (high SF) can activate dislocation
slip at lower applied stress compared with “hard-oriented” grains (low
SF). According to Schmid’s law, the critical resolved shear stress (τ )
required for slip system activation in FCC metals satisfies:
\sigma_ {\mathrm{a}} = \tau_ {\mathrm{c}} / \mu\tag{5}
where
\mu
is the Schmid factor and the
\sigma _ { \mathrm { a } }
is the applied tensile stress.
During cyclic deformation, dislocations are preferentially multiplicated
and glide in soft-oriented grains, leading to pile‑ups against boundaries
shared with hard‑oriented neighbors.
The dislocation distribution is clearly demonstrated by TEM char
acterizations of microstructures adjacent to grain boundaries after fa
tigue at a
\Delta \sigma / 2
of 315 MPa (Fig. 14). In the 550-6 sample (Fig. 14a),
κ-carbides are uniformly distributed within the grains, with no coarse
precipitation at the grain boundaries. These intragranular κ-carbides
facilitate organized planar slip bands, promoting relatively uniform slip
transfer across grain boundaries [26]. By contrast, the 650-6 sample
exhibits coarse intergranular κ-carbide precipitation disrupting the
continuity of grain boundaries (Fig. 14b). These brittle particles act as
strong slip barriers, intensifying dislocation pile-ups, promoting the
formation of tangled dislocation structures with wavy-slip patterns,
elevating local stress concentration, and eventually leading to earlier
crack nucleation and shortened fatigue life.
Based on the above analyses, the influence of intergranular κ-car
bides on the fatigue deformation mechanism is schematically illustrated
in Fig. 15. These differences in slip behavior directly correlate with the
fatigue performance at high stress amplitudes. In the 550-6 sample,
which has a homogeneous intragranular κ-carbide distribution and an
absence of intergranular κ-carbides, dislocation slip transfer is facili
tated and localization is suppressed. In the 650-6 sample, the presence of
severe intergranular κ-carbides impedes dislocation slip at grain
boundaries to cause severe dislocation pile-ups, exacerbates local stress
concentrations, and accelerates strain localization, leading to premature
crack initiation and failure. Consistently, the fatigue life ranking at high
amplitudes is 550-6 sample of best, 600-6 of intermediate, and 650-6 of
poorest, tracking the increasing severity of intergranular precipitation.
Apparently, such a detrimental grain boundary effect that offsets the size
benefit at low stress amplitudes discussed in Section 4.2 also degrades
fatigue resistance at high stress amplitudes by the same mechanism.
Based on the above analyses, achieving an optimal κ-carbide pre
cipitation state is essential for enhancing the fatigue performance of Fe-
Mn-Al-C austenitic low-density steels. This requires a critical balance,
namely, promoting a uniform distribution of intragranular κ-carbides
with an appropriate size, while effectively suppressing detrimental
precipitation at grain boundaries. Beneficial intragranular precipitates
improve fatigue strength and fatigue life at low stress amplitudes by
enhancing precipitation strengthening and dislocation slip reversibility.
In contrast, coarse intergranular κ-carbides significantly degrade fatigue
life at high stress amplitudes by accelerating stress concentration. Thus,
the superior overall fatigue properties can be effectively achieved
through microstructural control that maximizes the advantages of
intragranular precipitation and simultaneously minimizes the harmful
effects of intergranular precipitation.
